newsitem.title: USA: Orders rose at busy U.S. factories in April.
newsitem.headline: Orders rose at busy U.S. factories in April.

text.p: New orders to U.S. factories rose briskly in April as goods from airplanes to processed food were churned out at the fastest rate in a year, the government said Wednesday.
The value of new orders for all kinds of manufactured goods rose 1.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $323.9 billion after a revised 1.3 percent decline in March, the Commerce Department said.
Analysts said the report added to the impression of strength in the industrial sector after the first-quarter surge in economic growth.

"What it is telling us is that the momentum in the manufacturing sector is a lot stronger than it was expected to be at this point," said economist Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio.

But there were signs a slowdown could develop as order backlogs rose 0.3 percent in both March and April -- the first back-to-back monthly increases since mid-1995. And orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, fell 2 percent after a 3 percent plunge in March.
The pickup in April orders was the third rise in the past four months. Shipments also rose 1.2 percent, the fourth consecutive increase after a 0.1 percent March gain.
Department officials said it was the strongest monthly pickup in shipments in a year, since a 2.4 percent increase in April 1996.
Consumer demand was strong in the first quarter this year, when the economy grew at a brisk 5.8 percent annual rate, so some businesses may have been replenishing their depleted inventories.
"Manufacturers entered the second quarter on a high after benefiting from the surge in demand during the first quarter," said Philadelphia-based economist Joel Naroff of First Union Corp.
"But spending has been a disappointment and it is possible that factories overproduced early in this quarter," he added.
The government previously said sales at retail stores fell in April and Chrysler Corp. and other U.S. automakers have reported weaker year-over-year sales.
Inventories at manufacturing plants rose 0.6 percent during April to $445.7 billion after a 0.2 percent March gain, with most industry groups reporting some increase.
Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, said the report was "consistent with a slower but stable growth path" ahead.
"While inventories rose slightly, the inventory-shipments ratio declined," Jasinowski noted. "In other words, surplus stocks are being gradually worked off."
During April, orders for costly and long-lasting durable goods like new cars and refrigerators rose a revised 1.3 percent after a 2.2 percent drop in March.
Orders for non-durables like food and paper products increased 1 percent after a 0.3 percent decline in March.
The April factory orders report showed orders for transportation equipment rose 3.4 percent after a 3.9 percent decrease in March.
Shipments of motor vehicles and parts climbed 3.4 percent, more than recovering a 1.7 percent decline in March. In the automobile industry, shipments correspond to orders.
Excluding transportation, factory orders were up 0.9 percent in April after dropping 1 percent in March.

Manufacturing seems likely to remain brisk for some time to fill current orders. On Monday, the National Association of Purchasing Management said its index of industrial activity picked up briskly and unexpectedly in May, in large part because new orders continued to grow strongly.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, jumped 27.8 percent after a 12.2 percent drop March.
The March decline in factory orders was previously reported as a 1.6 percent drop.
